source.title: Hybrid Dual-Path Linear Transformations for Efficient Transformer Architectures

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites scaling-law work as background but does not test or rely on a scaling law as a method, baseline, or assumption in its experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper compares one dense model with one HDPL model, but does not sweep model parameters, training tokens, or compute to test a scaling relationship or extrapolation. Its architecture comparison also does not hold parameter count fixed, as V4 specifies.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as background in the introduction. Its one experiment compares a dense 67.11M model with a 62.53M HDPL variant at a single size and step count. There is no sweep over parameters, tokens or compute, no fitted law, and no extrapolation. The architecture change is a new operator type, not a depth/width shape variation at fixed parameter count, so it does not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that HDPL achieves lower validation loss (4.28 vs 4.32) with about 6.8% fewer parameters. They report roughly 44% lower throughput (270k vs 480k tokens/sec) in the current PyTorch/XLA implementation.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a new hybrid linear-layer architecture against a dense baseline; it does not reproduce a scaling-law fitting or compute-allocation method.

fits_no_version.finding: On FineWeb-Edu after 20k steps, the HDPL Surgical Hybrid (62.53M params) reaches validation loss 4.2838. The dense baseline (67.11M params) reaches 4.3206. Single seed, no uncertainty reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacing Q/K/V/Gate/Up projections with block-diagonal plus low-rank VAE operators lowers validation loss at fewer parameters in a small Llama-style model.

record.problems: Only one model size and one training run per architecture are reported; there is no scaling sweep or uncertainty estimate. The architecture comparison changes both the projection topology and total parameter count.

untested.parts: Power-law loss in parameters, tokens or compute; only one size per architecture.
Extrapolation from small-run fits to larger runs.
Effect of depth, width or shape at fixed parameter count. Both models share depth 4 and width 512, and the operator change also alters parameter count.
Downstream task performance versus scale or loss.
Sensitivity of exponents or compute-optimal split to fitting or setup choices.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r1 and r2 are correctly linked to none. The training-curve comparison (4.38 vs 4.44 at step 10k) is a method comparison, not scaling evidence, and needs no row.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss relationships across parameters, tokens, or compute, including over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of larger-run losses from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation across compute budgets.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count and across a wide range of depth, width, and other architectural choices.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits to setup and fitting choices, or departures from single power laws.

rows.subject: Surgical Hybrid (Ours)
rows.operation_detail: Trained the Llama-style model with HDPL replacing the Query, Key, Value, Gate, and Up projections.
rows.note: The paper reports 62.53M parameters for this model versus 67.11M for the dense baseline. This is a single architecture comparison, not a scaling sweep; parameter counts are not matched.

rows.subject: Baseline (Dense)
rows.operation_detail: Trained the standard Llama-style dense baseline.
rows.note: Comparator for the Surgical Hybrid model; this single result does not estimate a scaling relationship.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
